title: Breaking the Molecular Dynamics Timescale Barrier Using a Wafer-Scale System
problem: Molecular dynamics simulations on exascale supercomputers require excessive runtimes for systems and timescales of scientific interest, preventing access to slow microstructure transformation processes critical for material understanding.
motivation: Accessing previously inaccessible timescales in molecular dynamics simulations is critical for understanding material behavior and enabling breakthroughs in materials science, computational chemistry, biophysics, and drug design.
method: The system uses a Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine—a processor with thousands of cores densely packed together—and assigns one processor core to each atom being simulated. Because each atom can be processed independently, thousands of atoms get calculated in parallel rather than one after another. The system implements a dataflow algorithm (which moves data between cores only when needed) and uses the Embedded Atom Method physics model to calculate how atoms interact, allowing it to compute the time increments that molecular dynamics simulations require much faster than traditional supercomputers.
key_novelty: Mapping one processor core to each atom on a wafer-scale chip enables parallel molecular dynamics calculations.
contributions: 457x speedup over Frontier GPU-based exascale platform on molecular dynamics simulations
Achieves 699k timesteps per second for EAM simulations with up to 800k atoms
Reduces multi-year simulation runtimes to less than a day
Demonstrates strong scaling of MD on wafer-scale processors with general-purpose cores
